description: We are a small team of two Computer Science students participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge. We are interested in technology, coding, space exploration, and solving real-world problems. We look forward to learning new things, sharing ideas, and developing an innovative project together! 🚀
summary:
SPACE RELICS is an immersive, lightweight web-based educational platform that brings humanity's deactivated off-world space hardware back to life. Addressing the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge, we transform dry, technical telemetry from NASA's lunar and Martian monuments into compelling first-person humanized narratives.
The platform features an interactive Monument Archive with synthesized radio transmission playback, a Keplerian-physics Live Solar Orrery tracking orbital debris, a holographic Planetary Recon Radar mapping landing coordinates, and a gamified Explorer Studio where users customize 3D WebGL astronauts, complete scientific quizzes, and download personalized PDF reward dossiers.
By emotionally connecting school-age space enthusiasts to dormant rovers, landers, and probes, we bridge the gap between historic space achievements and the future of space exploration. Understanding past hardware weathering, material science, and orbital coordinates is crucial for the success of upcoming human settlements and missions like NASA's Artemis III.
details:
SPACE RELICS is built as an all-in-one interactive web application consisting of four key educational modules:

Monument Archive: Displays high-definition NASA imagery, hardware specifications, and imagined first-person sol logs for deep emotional storytelling. It features a built-in deep-space frequency interceptor that synthesizes spacecraft quotes into voice audio accompanied by radio static hiss.

Live Solar Orrery: An illustrative, physics-inspired 2D solar system where planets orbit on relative Keplerian speeds. Selecting Earth highlights Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) space debris, while selecting Mars or Moon lists human landing inventories.

Planetary Recon Radar: A rotating, holographic 3D wireframe globe scanner. Users select pulsing beacons to retrieve concise telemetry including lander mass, specific cause of mission termination, active instruments, and current preservation state.

Science & Future (2x2 Glassmorphism Grid): Bridges past spacecraft achievements directly to future missions (e.g., how Opportunity's water-ice discovery maps modern Artemis polar drills, and how Apollo retroreflectors aid the LunaNet lunar GPS network).

Gamification & Intended Impact

To heavily engage younger students, we integrated the Explorer Studio. Users customize an astronaut's skin, helmet, suit color, and mission gear with live WebGL previews. By exploring sections, they earn XP and unlock a 5-question scientific quiz. Passing the quiz awards the Master Explorer rank, enabling them to instantly download a personalized A4 PDF Reward Pack featuring a 3-view character sheet, collectible trading card, and graduation certificate. This gamification structure instills a personal connection and rewards active learning.

Technologies, Tools, & NASA Data Used

To ensure compatibility across school computers and mobile devices, we built the platform using lightweight, native HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and custom WebGL shaders with zero heavy external 3D engine dependencies. Personalized PDF generation is executed locally using jsPDF.

Scientific grounding is maintained by sourcing coordinates and flight logs from open NASA data archives, including the Planetary Photojournal, the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, and LEO statistics from the NASA Orbital Debris Program Office.

Team Considerations & Creativity

Our team focused on balancing scientific accuracy with emotional, anthropomorphic storytelling. By treating abandoned hardware not as space trash, but as "silent guardians" of human knowledge, we spark curiosity, teach complex material science, and inspire the next generation to support active space preservation laws under the Artemis Accords.
